tagline: Pine-covered buttes and trail landmarks along the Nebraska Panhandle
intro: The Gold Rush Byway follows U.S. 385 through the Nebraska Panhandle, from the South Dakota border to Colorado. Nebraska's Department of Transportation includes it among the state's scenic byways. The Nebraska Tourism Commission highlights pine-covered buttes, rolling hills and river valleys along the drive. Near Chadron, the Pine Ridge adds forested buttes, ridges and canyons carved from the high tableland.

An earlier road carried supplies toward the Black Hills gold fields. From 1876 to 1887, the Sidney Black Hills Stage Road connected Sidney and the Union Pacific Railroad with destinations including Custer City and Deadwood. It passed Courthouse and Jail Rocks and crossed the North Platte on Clarke Bridge. Rail connections replaced the trail in 1887; the present U.S. 385 designation first appeared in 1959.

Driving south from Chadron, pass the Pine Ridge country of Chadron State Park before continuing to Alliance. The park is wooded with ponderosa pine, with cottonwoods near the creek and lagoon. Carhenge stands north of Alliance. Alliance stands at the western edge of the Sand Hills. Cross the North Platte at Bridgeport, near Courthouse and Jail Rocks, then continue south to Sidney. U.S. 385 then shares U.S. 30 east to Chappell before turning south toward Colorado.

moments.title: Chadron
moments.text: Chadron moved to meet the railroad, taking its buildings along. Founder Fannie O'Linn had established the community, first called O'Linn, where Chadron Creek meets the White River. That was the expected railroad branch point. Instead, the tracks went to Bordeaux Creek, six miles away, and the town followed. The city now stands amid prairie grassland, with lightly forested hills to the south. The city's name honors Louis Chartran, a Métis fur trapper who ran a trading post on Chadron Creek in 1841. Near Chadron, the Museum of the Fur Trade occupies the site of the American Fur Company's former Bordeaux Trading Post.

moments.title: Carhenge
moments.text: A 1962 Cadillac takes the heelstone's place at Carhenge. Near Alliance, gray-painted American automobiles reproduce the shape of Stonehenge. Some cars stand trunk-down in five-foot pits; others are welded across their tops to form arches. Jim Reinders conceived the work in 1982 as a memorial to his father, who had lived on this farm. He had studied Stonehenge while living in England. Dedicated at the June 1987 summer solstice, the sculpture reproduces Stonehenge's surviving, incomplete form. Other sculptures made from cars have since joined it on the site, now called the Car Art Reserve.

moments.title: Courthouse and Jail Rocks
moments.text: Courthouse and Jail Rocks rise 240 feet above Pumpkin Creek near Bridgeport. Their clay, sandstone and volcanic ash are remnants of an ancient plateau split by the North Platte River. The Oregon-California, Mormon, Pony Express and Sidney-Deadwood trails all passed nearby. Travelers gave the formations architectural names: castles, a church and coffins appeared in descriptions before Courthouse and Jail became the most common. Hundreds of emigrants mentioned Courthouse Rock in their journals, recording the landmark as they traveled west. Some travelers left the Oregon Trail by as much as five miles to see the rocks.
